Seminar Title:

Anomaly Phase Transition of Gallium and Epitaxial Growth, Coalescence Mechanism of III-nitride Alloy by Molecular Dynamic Study

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Chemical Engineering

Speaker Name:

Anuj Debnath ( Rollno : 521ch1002)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

New seminar hall

Date and Time:

08 Jul 2026 10:30 AM

Contact:

Chandan Kumar Das

Abstract:

III-nitride semiconductor materials have emerged as one of the most promising material systems for advanced optoelectronic, electronic, and energy-related applications. It possesses direct and tuneable wide bandgaps, high thermal conductivity, excellent mechanical strength, and outstanding chemical stability. However, the performance of III-nitride-based devices are strongly influenced by atomic-scale defects such as phase transition, misfit dislocation, stacking faults, grain and domain boundaries, bulk voids, and surface pits. Atomic-scale study of phase transition and growth mechanism of III-nitride is essential for improving crystal quality and device performance. Growth mechanism of III-nitride involves, liquid phase epitaxy(LPE), molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), metalorganic chemical vapour deposition (MOCVD) etc. We performed Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate the anomalous solid-liquid phase transition behavior of gallium. Density change, radial distribution function (RDF), mean squared displacement (MSD), and diffusivity of gallium have been studied during the solid-liquid transition simulation. Subsequently, the &ldquoconstrained&nbsp&lambda&nbspintegration&rdquo method, coupled with multiple histogram reweighting (MHR) has been employed to determine the Gibbs free energy difference between the solid and liquid phases. Our findings indicate that the solid-liquid phase coexistence temperature of gallium is 305.2 &plusmn 1.2 K, which represents a significant improvement compared to previous simulations results. We successfully constructed the solid-liquid coexistence curve using the Gibbs-Duhem integration technique. The average slope of the solid-liquid transition line in the studied pressure region (0 to 1.8 GPa) was found to be -16.626 K/GPa. After that the MBE process has been simulated to understand the growth mechanism and defect formation in quaternary AInGaN and ternary AlGaN system using MD simulation. The influence of temperature and compositional variation on crystallinity, domain size, surface roughness, and dislocation defect formation was examined. Upon increasing the substrate temperature better crystallinity and reduced surface roughness was observed for both ternary and quaternary system. From the dislocation study, misfit dislocation with Burgers vector 1/3[12 10] and 1/3[11 00] were identified for both ternary and quaternary composite. The study of impact of Al/In ratio in quaternary system reveals that increase of Al/In ratio from 1/9 to 7/3 ratio reduce the lattice mismatch and increases the crystallinity domain size and reduces surface roughness. Impact of Al/Ga ratio in ternary AlxGa1-x N has been investigated for wide range of x values from 0.1 to 0.8. The surface roughness value increased slowly with an increase in Al content up to 0.6, but it rises sharply for Al content &gt 0.6 in ternary system. Formation of 3D columnar structure observed in both ternary and quaternary growth systems. Coalescence of these columnar structure is noticed after annealing, which improved the surface morphology and crystallinity. The coalescence mechanism of III-nitride nanoparticles has been studied by sintering InGaN nanoparticles as a model system. Key sintering metrics such as mean squared displacement (MSD), shrinkage ratio, neck growth rate, and dislocation formation were comprehensively evaluated. MSD analysis revealed that Zinc-blende phase nanoparticles exhibit higher atomic mobility than their Wurtzite counterparts. In heterogeneous sintering significant crystallographic phase transformation was observed for Zb-phase nanoparticles with radius R &lt 25 &Aring. The study demonstrated that coalescence behavior strongly depends on temperature and atomic diffusion kinetics. Overall, our MD simulation work provide fundamental insights into anomaly phase transition, growth mechanism, defect formation, which are important for the development of high-performance III-nitride materials for future electronic and optoelectronic applications.
